# The rhythms this brain is built to have

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/export_rhythms.py from ibm/rhythms.py.  Do not edit by hand:
     edit the catalogue and re-run, or the trainer and the prose will disagree. -->

A brain is not a box that maps inputs to outputs. It is a set of loops, each with an
anatomy, a conduction budget and a band it lives in, and this file is the list of the ones
IBM-1 is being built to have. It is a **specification**: the programme is a construction,
not a search (see `CLAUDE.md`, "Construction, not search"), so these are written down
first and the substrate is shaped toward them.

Three things read the same table, and that is the point of generating this file rather
than writing it:

- `scripts/shape_rhythms.py` turns each entry into a term in the training objective,
  through the differentiable spectral instrument in `ibm/spectral.py`. The spectrum is a
  **pressure during gradient descent**, alongside the anatomical and tractometric ones —
  not something measured afterwards to see where the model happened to land.
- the measurement scripts read the same `measure` spec, so reading a rhythm off real EEG
  and reading it off the model is one code path with two inputs.
- `site/data/rhythms.js`, and through it the resonance section of the site.

## What the evidence column means

| tag | meaning | count |
|---|---|---|
| `measured-here` | fitted in this repo on held-out subjects; the row names the script and the number | 3 |
| `measurable-now` | the corpus is on disk and the instrument exists; nobody has run it | 4 |
| `literature` | declared from published physiology, no local measurement | 26 |
| `target` | what we intend the substrate to produce; nothing measured at this specificity | 20 |

Only **3** rows have been through anything in this repository that could have
said no. The rest are declarations, and the column is there so that no reader — including
a future one of us — can mistake the table's completeness for evidence.

`substrate` says what the **model** would need before a row could be scored at all.
`ibm/substrate.py` is a cortical field: 9 of 53 rows are expressible
on it today. A rhythm whose loop runs through the reticular nucleus, the subthalamic
nucleus or the spinal cord is not expressible by a cortical sheet, and scoring its band in
cortex anyway would produce a number that moves for the wrong reason.

## The round-trip bound

A loop cannot oscillate faster than it can go round. With a total round-trip delay `D`
(conduction plus synaptic, summed over the ring), a net-inhibitory loop is bounded by
`f <= 1/(2D)` and a net-excitatory one by `f <= 1/D`.

This is a **ceiling, never a prediction** — most of these frequencies are set by membrane
and synaptic time constants, with the delay far from binding. It is in the table because
it is the one law the table can check against itself, and it earns its place: on the first
run it caught two rhythms filed under the wrong loop (Purkinje synchrony at 200 Hz and
olfactory gamma at 70 Hz were both attached to long loops, when both are produced by local
reciprocal circuits), and one genuine conflict that is now declared as an exception with
its reason (the Piper rhythm). `python ibm/rhythms.py` runs every check.

## Loop by loop

### thalamo-cortico-thalamic

The loop the whole brain integrates through: cortex drives thalamus, and thalamus drives cortex back.

Ring: mediodorsal thalamus → dorsolateral prefrontal cortex → thalamic reticular nucleus → mediodorsal thalamus. Round trip 5–11 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 45–100 Hz.

- **cortical slow oscillation** (0.5–1.5 Hz, peak 0.8 Hz, `literature`). Adaptation and synaptic depression drain an up state until the cortex falls silent, and recover until it ignites again. The period is the recovery time, not a delay. *The one rhythm the v2 substrate can already produce unaided: tau_a runs 0.30-1.20 s across the hierarchy, which is the right range for a 0.5-1.5 Hz up/down cycle.* [Steriade 1993; Sanchez-Vives & McCormick 2000]
- **thalamocortical delta** (1–4 Hz, peak 2 Hz, `literature`). The relay cell's own T-type calcium current and h-current alternate burst and pause when it is hyperpolarised; the cortex follows. [McCormick & Pape 1990; Steriade 1993]
- **sleep spindles** (11–16 Hz, peak 13.45 Hz, `measured-here`). The reticular nucleus inhibits the relay cells, they rebound through the T-current, and they drive the reticular nucleus again. The frequency is set by the GABA-B decay and the de-inactivation time of the T-current. *MEASURED: scripts/fit_sleep_resonance.py fitted the declared alpha_resonator to N2 spectra split by subject; the centre moved off its 10 Hz prior to 13.452 Hz on held-out people, +5503.2 nats/night, p = 7.2e-11. The only fitted frequency in this table.* [Steriade 1993; Luthi 2014]
- **spindles nested in the slow oscillation** (11–16 Hz, `measurable-now`). Spindles do not fall anywhere in the slow oscillation: they ride its up-state phase. The nesting is the mechanism memory consolidation is attributed to, so it is a target in its own right and not a by-product of getting both bands right. *Two right bands with no coupling between them is the failure mode this entry exists to catch: a model can score both power terms and still have them independent.* [Staresina 2015; Helfrich 2018]
- **K-complex** (0.5–1.5 Hz, `literature`). A single evoked down state: the slow oscillation's machinery fired once by a stimulus rather than free-running. *An evoked event, not a band. It is here because a substrate that produces the slow oscillation but cannot be made to produce ONE on demand has the rhythm without the mechanism.* [Cash 2009]

### cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamo-cortical

Motor and premotor cortex propose; the striatum and pallidum release one proposal and suppress the rest; the thalamus returns the winner.

Ring: premotor and supplementary motor cortex → striatum → internal pallidum → ventroanterior thalamus → premotor and supplementary motor cortex. Round trip 10–23 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 43–100 Hz.

- **prokinetic striatal gamma** (60–90 Hz, peak 75 Hz, `literature`). A fast rhythm that appears in the striatum and subthalamic nucleus at movement onset -- the opposite polarity to beta. [Jenkinson 2013]
- **one proposal released, the rest suppressed** (—, `target`). Not a band at all: the loop's actual job. Several cortical proposals arrive, the pallidum's tonic inhibition lifts off exactly one, and the thalamus returns it. *Here to keep the table honest: a loop is specified by what it computes, not only by the frequency it hums at, and a model that reproduced every band in this file while selecting nothing would have missed the point.* [Redgrave 1999; Mink 1996]

### subthalamo-pallidal pacemaker

The reciprocal STN-GPe pair, the fastest loop in the basal ganglia and the one whose synchrony is read out as pathological beta.

Ring: subthalamic nucleus → external pallidum → subthalamic nucleus. Round trip 5–9 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 56–100 Hz.

- **basal-ganglia beta** (13–30 Hz, peak 20 Hz, `literature`). The subthalamo-pallidal pair is a delayed inhibitory loop with a natural period in the beta range, and cortex entrains it. High beta means hold; movement suppresses it. *The bound: 5-9 ms net inhibitory gives f <= 56-100 Hz, so the delay does not set beta here -- the synaptic time constants do. Worth knowing before anyone tunes a delay to get the band.* [Brown 2001; Kuhn 2006; Jenkinson & Brown 2011]
- **beta arrives in bursts, not as a tone** (13–30 Hz, `literature`). Averaged beta power is an artefact of averaging: the real signal is bursts of 100-500 ms whose RATE and DURATION carry the state, and long bursts are what correlates with slowness in Parkinson's disease. *The entry that stops a power target from being satisfied the wrong way: a constant 13-30 Hz tone scores the same band power as real bursting and is not the same object.* [Tinkhauser 2017; Feingold 2015]

### hippocampal-entorhinal

Entorhinal input rides a slow theta cycle, and each cycle is divided into faster gamma slots.

Ring: parahippocampal and entorhinal cortex → dentate gyrus → CA3 → CA1 → subiculum → parahippocampal and entorhinal cortex. Round trip 12–29 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 34–83 Hz.

- **hippocampal theta** (3–8 Hz, peak 6 Hz, `literature`). The septal pacemaker and the entorhinal-hippocampal loop together; in humans it is slower and burstier than the rodent's continuous 8 Hz. *The bound is instructive: the entorhinal ring is 12-29 ms excitatory, f <= 34-83 Hz. Theta is nowhere near it, which is why the septal pacemaker is in the table -- the ring alone would ring far too fast.* [Buzsaki 2002; Jacobs 2014]
- **gamma nested in theta** (30–100 Hz, `target`). Each theta cycle is divided into gamma slots, and what fires in which slot is the order of the episode. This is the entry the whole loop is for: sequence carried by WHEN, not stored beside the item as an index. [Lisman & Jensen 2013; Tort 2009; Colgin 2009]
- **entorhinal-driven fast gamma** (60–100 Hz, peak 80 Hz, `literature`). The faster gamma CA1 shows when the entorhinal cortex is driving it -- the encoding mode. Two gammas, two sources, one region: the pair is the evidence that the region is switching between inputs rather than running one oscillator. [Colgin 2009]
- **ripples inside spindles inside slow oscillations** (140–200 Hz, `target`). The triple nesting: hippocampal ripples fall inside the troughs of thalamic spindles, which fall on the up state of the cortical slow oscillation. Three loops, three bands, one hierarchy -- the mechanism consolidation is attributed to. *The most demanding entry here, and the one that would say most: it cannot be satisfied by tuning any single loop.* [Staresina 2015; Latchoumane 2017]
- **phase precession** (3–8 Hz, `target`). A place cell fires progressively earlier in the theta cycle as the animal crosses its field, so position is read out from PHASE rather than from rate. *Needs a body that goes somewhere, which is the whole programme's target, so this entry is a milestone as much as a rhythm.* [O'Keefe & Recce 1993; Mehta 2002]

### CA3-CA1 local circuit

The local recurrent circuit that a sharp wave detonates; too short to be anything but fast.

Ring: CA3 → CA1 → CA3. Round trip 2.5–5 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 100–200 Hz.

- **CA3-driven slow gamma** (25–55 Hz, peak 40 Hz, `literature`). The slow gamma CA1 shows when CA3 is driving it -- the retrieval mode. [Colgin 2009]
- **sharp-wave ripples** (140–200 Hz, peak 170 Hz, `target`). A CA3 population burst detonates CA1 and the local interneurons ring at 150-200 Hz for 50-100 ms. Sequences replay inside one, compressed twentyfold. *The fastest entry in the table, and the bound is the reason it is possible at all: the CA3-CA1 local loop is 2.5-5 ms net inhibitory, f <= 100-200 Hz. It only just fits, which is the point -- nothing longer could produce a ripple.* [Buzsaki 2015; Csicsvari 1999]

### fronto-parietal dorsal attention

Occipito-temporal cortex proposes what is worth looking at, parietal cortex holds the map it is proposed on, and frontal cortex commits to one place.

Ring: extrastriate visual cortex → intraparietal / superior parietal cortex → frontal eye field → extrastriate visual cortex. Round trip 26–50 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 20–38 Hz.

- **attention samples rhythmically** (4–8 Hz, peak 7 Hz, `target`). Sustained attention is not sustained: behavioural performance at an attended location waxes and wanes at 4-8 Hz, in antiphase between two objects. [Landau & Fries 2012; Fiebelkorn 2018]
- **alpha takes sides** (8–13 Hz, `measurable-now`). Attend left and alpha rises in the left hemisphere, gating out the ignored side. The goal is that visual salience is a competition running inside the substrate, not a saliency map bolted on. *ds008037's working-memory task is lateralised, so this is measurable on data already on disk -- unlike the single-trial decoding the withdrawn step 2 attempted, a lateralisation index is a within-subject contrast and does not need trial-level stimulus information.* [Worden 2000; Thut 2006]
- **attentional gamma** (40–70 Hz, `target`). Attending to a stimulus raises gamma coherence between the areas representing it -- communication through coherence. [Fries 2015; Bosman 2012]

### salience and medial frontal control

The anterior insula and cingulate mark what matters and hand control the need to change course.

Ring: insular cortex → anterior cingulate cortex → dorsolateral prefrontal cortex → insular cortex. Round trip 17–40 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 25–59 Hz.

- **frontal midline theta** (4–8 Hz, peak 6 Hz, `measurable-now`). Medial frontal cortex runs a theta rhythm that grows with how much is being held and with how much control is needed; it is the clearest cortical signature of effort. *MEASURABLE ON WHAT WE HOLD: ds008037 has 111 subjects, set sizes 2/4/6, and the extracted delay-period features. Theta power against set size is a within-subject slope -- exactly the kind of contrast that survives where trial-level decoding did not.* [Cavanagh & Frank 2014; Jensen & Tesche 2002]
- **error and feedback theta** (4–8 Hz, peak 6 Hz, `measurable-now`). A burst of medial frontal theta follows an error or a worse-than-expected outcome, within about 200 ms. [Cavanagh 2012]

### amygdala-vmPFC-accumbens valuation

The amygdala scores what has just arrived, ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the anterior cingulate revise that score against context, and the accumbens turns it into a pull toward or away.

Ring: amygdala → ventromedial prefrontal cortex → nucleus accumbens → ventral tegmental area → amygdala. Round trip 29–69 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 7–17 Hz.

- **feedback theta and delta** (2–8 Hz, peak 5 Hz, `literature`). A reward or its absence is followed by a low-frequency response over medial frontal cortex whose size tracks how surprising the outcome was. [Cavanagh & Frank 2014; Holroyd & Coles 2002]
- **amygdala-prefrontal theta coherence** (4–8 Hz, `target`). Under threat, the amygdala and ventromedial prefrontal cortex lock in theta, and which one leads is the difference between being gripped by a thing and appraising it. *The goal is that value is a state of a brain attached to a body, not a scalar handed in from outside it.* [Likhtik 2014]
- **accumbens gamma** (50–100 Hz, `target`). Fast oscillations in the accumbens that shift band with approach and consumption. [van der Meer & Redish 2009]

### cerebello-thalamo-cortical

Motor cortex sends a copy of each command through the pons to the cerebellum, which returns a correction through the thalamus before the movement has finished.

Ring: primary motor cortex → pontine nuclei → cerebellar cortex → dentate nucleus → ventrolateral thalamus → primary motor cortex. Round trip 17–42 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 12–29 Hz.

- **physiological tremor** (8–12 Hz, peak 10 Hz, `literature`). A limb held against gravity oscillates at around 10 Hz, and the olivo-cerebellar clock is one of the things that sets it. [Elble & Koller 1990; Llinas 1988]
- **cerebello-cortical coherence** (13–30 Hz, `target`). During steady posture the cerebellum and motor cortex share beta, and the correction arrives before the movement has finished. The goal is timing that comes from the loop, not from a tuned controller. [Gross 2002]

### olivo-cerebellar timing

The inferior olive's electrically coupled cells fire together and stamp a clock on the cerebellar cortex, one complex spike at a time.

Ring: inferior olive → cerebellar cortex → dentate nucleus → inferior olive. Round trip 10–24 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 42–100 Hz.

- **olivary complex-spike rhythm** (5–10 Hz, peak 8 Hz, `literature`). The inferior olive's cells are electrically coupled and oscillate subthreshold near 10 Hz, so complex spikes arrive on a clock rather than at random. [Llinas & Yarom 1986; Welsh 1995]

### default-mode network

Posterior cingulate, precuneus, medial prefrontal and angular cortex rise together when nothing outside demands attention.

Ring: posterior cingulate and precuneus → ventromedial prefrontal cortex → angular gyrus → posterior cingulate and precuneus. Round trip 32–68 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 15–31 Hz.

- **default-mode infraslow coupling** (0.01–0.1 Hz, peak 0.05 Hz, `literature`). Posterior cingulate, medial prefrontal and angular cortex rise and fall together over tens of seconds when nothing outside demands attention. The goal is a resting brain with structure -- recollection and self-reference -- rather than a model that idles. *Expressible in principle and expensive in practice: 0.01 Hz needs runs of several minutes of simulated time to have any frequency resolution at all.* [Raichle 2001; Fox 2005]

### auditory thalamocortical

Cochlea, brainstem, medial geniculate and Heschl's gyrus, each station locking to the timing of the sound.

Ring: medial geniculate nucleus → primary auditory cortex → medial geniculate nucleus. Round trip 4–9 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 111–250 Hz.

- **40 Hz auditory steady-state response** (38–42 Hz, peak 40 Hz, `literature`). Click trains near 40 Hz get a disproportionate response: the thalamocortical auditory loop's own resonance. *I first wrote this entry claiming the conduction budget PREDICTS 40 Hz, by counting the ring twice to make the arithmetic come out. It does not: the A1-MGN ring is 4-9 ms, so the bound is 111-250 Hz and nowhere near binding. The 40 Hz preference is set by synaptic and rebound time constants, like most of this table. The bound is a ceiling, never a prediction, and the first draft of this file is what happens when that is forgotten.* [Galambos 1981; Picton 2003]
- **auditory cortical gamma** (30–80 Hz, `literature`). The local E/I loop in auditory cortex, the same machinery as visual gamma with a different input. [Brosch 2002]

### cochlea to cortex

The ascending path, which is a delay line rather than a loop: it sets when a sound arrives, not what rhythm it arrives in.

Ring: cochlea → medial geniculate nucleus → primary auditory cortex. Round trip 6–15 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 67–167 Hz.

- **cortical tracking of the speech envelope** (1–8 Hz, `target`). Auditory cortex follows the slow amplitude envelope of speech, at the rate of syllables. The goal is that speech is followed by a loop that entrains to it, not by a spectrogram handed in from outside. [Ding & Simon 2014; Gross 2013]

### brainstem-thalamic arousal

The ascending arousal system sets how the thalamus gates the cortex, and so whether the brain is awake, drowsy or asleep.

Ring: locus coeruleus → thalamic reticular nucleus → mediodorsal thalamus → dorsolateral prefrontal cortex → locus coeruleus. Round trip 27–75 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 13–37 Hz.

- **infraslow arousal fluctuation** (0.01–0.1 Hz, `literature`). A global fluctuation in excitability, locked to pupil size and to noradrenergic tone. [Aston-Jones & Cohen 2005; Raut 2021]
- **ponto-geniculo-occipital waves** (0.5–2 Hz, `target`). Bursts that leave the pons, pass through the geniculate and reach occipital cortex during REM: the visual system driven from inside. [Datta 1997]

### REM-on / REM-off flip-flop

Two mutually inhibiting brainstem populations; the brain is in one state or the other and crosses between them on a ninety-minute cycle.

Ring: pedunculopontine / laterodorsal tegmentum → locus coeruleus → pedunculopontine / laterodorsal tegmentum. Round trip 20–60 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 17–50 Hz.

- **the REM/NREM cycle** (1.50e-04–2.50e-04 Hz, peak 1.85e-04 Hz, `target`). Two mutually inhibiting brainstem populations hold the brain in REM or in NREM and flip between them roughly every ninety minutes. The goal is that sleep and waking are states the substrate moves between, not modes chosen by a flag. [Saper 2001; Lu 2006]

### retino-geniculo-striate

Retina to the lateral geniculate to striate cortex and out into the visual hierarchy, with the thalamus gating what gets through.

Ring: retina → lateral geniculate nucleus → primary visual cortex → lateral geniculate nucleus → thalamic reticular nucleus → lateral geniculate nucleus. Round trip 14–33 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 15–36 Hz.

- **occipital alpha** (8–13 Hz, peak 10 Hz, `measured-here`). The geniculo-cortical loop with the reticular gate closed on it. Eyes closed, the loop rings; eyes open, the retinal drive breaks it. *MEASURED as a two-state contrast on 44 held-out subjects: the declared occipital alpha resonator beats a 1/f background by +201.6 and the eyes-open/eyes-closed contrast by +200.4; the relabelling control collapses. Moving the centre OFF its 10 Hz prior FAILED -- the prior is already where the data wants it.* [Lopes da Silva 1991; Klimesch 1999]
- **alpha blocking on eye opening** (8–13 Hz, `measured-here`). The same loop in two states. Berger's observation, and the cleanest state contrast in electrophysiology. *A ratio, and the reason this loop is worth more than a power target: a model can be given an alpha peak by hand, but it cannot be given one that switches off when the eyes open unless the gating is real.* [Berger 1929; Barry 2007]
- **alpha as a travelling wave** (8–13 Hz, `literature`). Alpha is not a standing hum: its phase sweeps across the cortical sheet, mostly occipital to frontal, at a few metres per second. *This is the term that makes the substrate's conduction delays load-bearing: a sheet with instantaneous coupling can have the band and cannot have the wave.* [Halgren 2019; Zhang 2018]
- **steady-state visual entrainment** (4–60 Hz, `literature`). A flickering stimulus drags the visual loop to its own frequency, and the response appears at that frequency and its harmonics. *The calibration rhythm of this table. Drive at f, get a peak at f: any instrument or substrate that fails THIS is broken in a way that has nothing to do with physiology.* [Norcia 2015]

### Purkinje and molecular-layer interneurons

The cerebellar cortex's own reciprocal circuit: Purkinje cells and the basket and stellate cells that silence them, a loop short enough to ring at 200 Hz.

Ring: cerebellar cortex → cerebellar cortex → cerebellar cortex. Round trip 1–3 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 167–500 Hz.

- **Purkinje simple-spike synchrony** (160–250 Hz, peak 200 Hz, `literature`). Neighbouring Purkinje cells fire simple spikes in near-lockstep at 200 Hz, which is how the cerebellar cortex carries fine timing rather than rate. [de Solages 2008; De Zeeuw 2011]

### mitral-granule dendrodendritic loop

Mitral cells excite granule cells through dendrodendritic synapses and are inhibited back across the same contact: the olfactory bulb's gamma generator.

Ring: olfactory bulb → olfactory bulb → olfactory bulb. Round trip 2–5 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 100–250 Hz.

- **olfactory bulb gamma** (40–100 Hz, peak 70 Hz, `target`). Mitral cells and granule cells form a reciprocal loop that rings at gamma on each inhalation. [Kay 2009]

### local cortical excitation-inhibition

Pyramidal cells excite fast interneurons and the interneurons silence them a few milliseconds later: the smallest loop in the cortex and the fastest.

Ring: primary visual cortex → primary visual cortex → primary visual cortex. Round trip 3–8 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 62–167 Hz.

- **visual gamma** (30–80 Hz, peak 50 Hz, `literature`). Pyramidal cells excite fast interneurons, the interneurons silence them, and the cycle is the interneuron's decay. Frequency rises with contrast: it is a property of the drive, not a fixed clock. *The E/I loop that produces it is exactly what `ibm/substrate.py` is, so this is the second rhythm the cortical sheet could own today -- but tau_I is 5 ms, which puts the natural PING frequency near 60-80 Hz, and nothing has checked where it actually lands.* [Buzsaki & Wang 2012; Ray & Maunsell 2010]

### sensorimotor mu

Sensorimotor cortex idles in a rhythm that breaks the moment a movement is planned, made or watched.

Ring: ventroposterior thalamus → primary somatosensory cortex → primary motor cortex → ventroposterior thalamus → thalamic reticular nucleus → ventroposterior thalamus. Round trip 9–22 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 23–56 Hz.

- **sensorimotor mu** (8–13 Hz, peak 10 Hz, `literature`). The somatosensory arm of the same thalamocortical machinery that makes occipital alpha, idling over the central sulcus. *FAILED once already, and the failure was the DECLARATION, not the data: the declared resonator was a low-pass form that cannot fit a small peak on a steep background. A band-pass declaration is owed a fresh pre-registration before it is fitted again.* [Pfurtscheller 1999; Hari 2006]
- **mu breaking on movement** (8–13 Hz, `literature`). The rhythm desynchronises before the muscle moves, and on watching someone else move. *The goal is that preparing to act shows in the loop before any muscle moves -- which means this entry cannot be scored until the substrate is attached to a body that can be about to move.* [Pfurtscheller & Lopes da Silva 1999]
- **post-movement beta rebound** (15–30 Hz, peak 20 Hz, `literature`). Beta collapses during the movement and overshoots its baseline for a second afterwards. [Jurkiewicz 2006]

### cortico-muscular-spinal

Motor cortex drives the motoneuron pool, the muscle answers, and the spindle afferents carry the answer back -- the shortest loop that leaves the head.

Ring: primary motor cortex → alpha motoneuron pools → skeletal muscle (EMG) → muscle spindle afferents → primary somatosensory cortex → primary motor cortex. Round trip 35–57 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 18–29 Hz.

- **corticomuscular coherence** (15–30 Hz, peak 20 Hz, `literature`). During a held contraction the motor cortex and the muscle it drives share a beta rhythm, and the coherence between cortex and EMG is the most direct evidence that the loop is closed. *The round-trip bound nearly binds here and it is worth saying out loud: the loop is ~35-57 ms and net excitatory, so f <= 18-29 Hz. Beta is where the loop CAN ring.* [Conway 1995; Salenius 1997; Baker 2007]
- **Piper rhythm** (30–60 Hz, peak 40 Hz, `literature`). The same coupling at a higher band during strong contractions. *Sits ABOVE the cortico-muscular round-trip bound, so whatever it is, it is not that loop resonating.* **Bound exemption:** 40 Hz needs a round trip under 25 ms and the cortico-muscular loop is 35-57 ms. Declared as an exception rather than dropped: the coupling is measured, so the loop it is assigned to here is wrong, probably a shorter subcortical or intraspinal path we have not written down. [Brown 1998]

### monosynaptic stretch reflex

Spindle to motoneuron and straight back out: the loop that does not consult the brain.

Ring: muscle spindle afferents → alpha motoneuron pools → skeletal muscle (EMG) → muscle spindle afferents. Round trip 15–29 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 34–67 Hz.

- **the stretch reflex's own resonance** (6–12 Hz, peak 9 Hz, `literature`). The monosynaptic loop from spindle to motoneuron and back through the muscle has a round trip near 20-30 ms, which is a resonance whether or not anything wants one -- it is one of the things a limb's tremor is made of. [Lippold 1970; Matthews 1997]

### spinal locomotor central pattern generator

Half-centres in the cord that alternate flexor and extensor drive on their own, with the brainstem setting only how fast.

Ring: mesencephalic locomotor region → lumbar central pattern generator → lumbar central pattern generator → alpha motoneuron pools. Round trip 15–40 ms, net inhibitory, ceiling 12–33 Hz.

- **the locomotor rhythm** (0.5–3 Hz, peak 1.2 Hz, `target`). Half-centres in the cord alternate flexor and extensor drive with no rhythmic input at all; the brainstem drive sets only how fast. The crawling body this programme is for moves because of this loop or it does not move. *The frequency must be a MONOTONIC function of the descending drive with the phase relationship unchanged -- that is the actual specification, not the band.* [Grillner 2006; Kiehn 2016]
- **flexor and extensor in antiphase** (0.5–3 Hz, `target`). The two half-centres are half a cycle apart, and left and right are too. A pattern generator that produced the right frequency in phase would be no pattern generator. [Kiehn 2016]

### gut-vagus-insula interoception

The stomach's own pacemaker, carried up the vagus, read in the insula: a rhythm the brain does not generate and cannot ignore.

Ring: stomach pacemaker (interstitial cells of Cajal) → nucleus of the solitary tract → parabrachial nucleus → ventroposterior thalamus → insular cortex. Round trip 262–536 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 2–4 Hz.

- **the gastric rhythm** (0.045–0.055 Hz, peak 0.05 Hz, `target`). The stomach's interstitial cells of Cajal fire at three cycles a minute whatever the brain does, and a network of cortical regions is phase-locked to them. *IBM-1 already declares the vagal path this rides: 448 ms on unmyelinated C fibres, re-measured after the relay fix. The rhythm is the body's, not the brain's, which is exactly why it belongs in a brain built to be attached to one.* [Rebollo 2018; Richter 2017]
- **the heartbeat-evoked response** (1–1.5 Hz, `target`). Every heartbeat produces a cortical response in insula and somatosensory cortex, whose size tracks how much attention is on the body. [Park 2014; Al 2020]

### respiratory-olfactory-limbic

Breathing paces the olfactory bulb, and the bulb paces the structures behind it, so the body's slowest motor act shows up as a cortical rhythm.

Ring: pre-Botzinger complex → diaphragm and lungs → olfactory bulb → parahippocampal and entorhinal cortex → CA1. Round trip 65–177 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 6–15 Hz.

- **breathing paces the brain** (0.15–0.4 Hz, peak 0.25 Hz, `target`). Nasal airflow drives the olfactory bulb and, behind it, entorhinal cortex, hippocampus and amygdala; memory and reaction time vary with the phase of the breath. [Zelano 2016; Herrero 2018]

### suprachiasmatic circadian

A transcriptional clock with a period near a day, which every other rhythm here is nested inside.

Ring: suprachiasmatic nucleus → locus coeruleus → suprachiasmatic nucleus. Round trip 40–120 ms, net excitatory, ceiling 8–25 Hz.

- **the circadian cycle** (1.00e-05–1.30e-05 Hz, peak 1.16e-05 Hz, `target`). A transcriptional clock with a period near 24 hours, which every other rhythm in this table is nested inside. *Out of reach of any simulation that runs for seconds, and in the table because a brain without it has no reason to sleep.* [Reppert & Weaver 2002]

## The loops, and their conduction budgets

Round trips are the sum over the ring of declared conduction plus synaptic delay, as an
interval. The ceiling is what the round-trip bound allows.

## Stations that do not exist yet

The atlas addresses 65 stations, and some of the ones these loops need are
inside a blob or absent altogether. Listed here rather than glossed, because a loop drawn
through a structure the model cannot address is a loop the model cannot have:

- **primary auditory cortex** (`a1`) — Heschl's gyrus; core and belt are not separated
- **premotor and supplementary motor cortex** (`pmc`) — SMA is inside paracentral/superiorfrontal
- **intraparietal / superior parietal cortex** (`ips`) — IPS is a sulcus, not a DK label
- **frontal eye field** (`fef`) — FEF is not a DK label; it sits at this junction
- **insular cortex** (`insula`) — posterior (interoceptive) and anterior (salience) insula are one label here
- **angular gyrus** (`ang`) — angular and supramarginal share inferiorparietal in DK
- **thalamic reticular nucleus** (`trn`) — TRN is a shell around the thalamus; not separable in this atlas
- **lateral geniculate nucleus** (`lgn`) — inside `thalamus`
- **medial geniculate nucleus** (`mgn`) — inside `thalamus`
- **ventrolateral thalamus** (`vl`) — the cerebellar-recipient motor nucleus; inside `thalamus`
- **ventroanterior thalamus** (`va_vl_bg`) — the pallidal-recipient nucleus; inside `thalamus`
- **mediodorsal thalamus** (`md`) — inside `thalamus`
- **pulvinar** (`pulvinar`) — inside `thalamus`
- **ventroposterior thalamus** (`vpl`) — somatosensory relay; inside `thalamus`
- **external pallidum** (`gpe`) — GPe and GPi are one `pallidum` label
- **internal pallidum** (`gpi`) — see GPe
- **subthalamic nucleus** (`stn`) — NO label at all: the STN is absent from this atlas
- **substantia nigra pars compacta** (`snc`) — inside the `brainstem` blob
- **dentate gyrus** (`dg`) — inside the `hippocampus` blob
- **CA3** (`ca3`) — inside the `hippocampus` blob
- **CA1** (`ca1`) — inside the `hippocampus` blob
- **subiculum** (`sub`) — inside the `hippocampus` blob
- **medial septum / diagonal band** (`ms`) — NO label: the septal theta pacemaker is absent from this atlas
- **cerebellar cortex** (`cb_ctx`) — one blob: no lobules, no Purkinje/granule layers
- **dentate nucleus** (`dentate_n`) — inside `cerebellum`
- **pontine nuclei** (`pons`) — inside the `brainstem` blob
- **inferior olive** (`io`) — inside the `brainstem` blob
- **locus coeruleus** (`lc`) — inside the `brainstem` blob
- **dorsal raphe** (`raphe`) — inside the `brainstem` blob
- **pedunculopontine / laterodorsal tegmentum** (`ppt`) — the cholinergic REM-on group; inside `brainstem`
- **ventral tegmental area** (`vta`) — inside `brainstem`
- **nucleus of the solitary tract** (`nts`) — first visceral relay; inside `brainstem`
- **parabrachial nucleus** (`pb`) — inside `brainstem`
- **superior colliculus** (`sc_coll`) — inside `brainstem`
- **pre-Botzinger complex** (`preBotC`) — the respiratory rhythm generator; inside `brainstem`
- **suprachiasmatic nucleus** (`scn`) — NO label: the circadian clock is absent from this atlas
- **nucleus basalis** (`nbm`) — NO label; cholinergic basal forebrain
- **mesencephalic locomotor region** (`mlr`) — inside `brainstem`
- **olfactory bulb** (`ob`) — NO label in this atlas
- **lumbar central pattern generator** (`cord_lumbar`) — the CPG is a distributed interneuron network, not a segment
- **skeletal muscle (EMG)** (`muscle`) — IHM-1 owns the muscles; the EEG/MEG graph has no body
- **muscle spindle afferents** (`spindle_afferent`) — IHM-1
- **stomach pacemaker (interstitial cells of Cajal)** (`gut`) — IHM-1
- **heart** (`heart`) — IHM-1
- **diaphragm and lungs** (`lung`) — IHM-1
